title: MB9-16273
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): On appeal, the appellant submits that the RPD did not assess her testimony with caution, that it was overzealous and that its reasons are not sufficient to rebut the presumption of truth.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I allow the appeal.
The appellant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Haiti, where she fears for her life as a survivor of domestic violence.
The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected the appellant's refugee protection claim because it found that her testimony was not credible.
On appeal, the appellant submits that the RPD did not assess her testimony with caution, that it was overzealous and that its reasons are not sufficient to rebut the presumption of truth.
The determinative issue in this appeal is the appellant's credibility.

My role is to review all the evidence, including the hearing recording, and to determine whether the RPD decision is correct.1 I considered Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Fearing Gender-Related Persecution (Guideline 4) in my analysis of this refugee protection claim. The Refugee Protection Division erred in assessing the appellant's credibility

The RPD decided that the appellant did not credibly establish that she had experienced domestic abuse at the hands of her ex-spouse in Haiti, against whom she did not file a complaint as he was the police commissioner in her neighbourhood. Its conclusion is based on the following contradictions and inconsistencies that the appellant was allegedly unable to justify [translation] "to the panel's satisfaction": * There were variations between two of the letters submitted at the hearing and versions submitted earlier. * The appellant's behaviour was inconsistent with that of a person genuinely fearing for her life because she chose to return to Haiti after staying in the United States and the Dominican Republic,. * The appellant's passport contained stamps for trips that she had not reported. * In the appellant's spontaneous statement made upon arriving in Canada, she alleged that she worked during the period when she claimed to have been hiding at a female friend's house. * The medical certificate submitted into evidence states that the appellant's left eye was injured, while the appellant claimed that her right eye was injured.

I do not agree that these inconsistencies are sufficient to conclude that the appellant was not a victim of abuse at the hands of her ex-spouse. Here is why. The variations between the letters submitted at the hearing and those submitted earlier

Contrary to the RPD, I am of the view that the appellant's explanation for the variations between the letters submitted at the hearing and those submitted earlier, namely, that she asked the authors to correct spelling errors, is satisfactory.2 I draw no negative inference from the fact that the contents of these letters differed slightly; it is reasonable to believe that the letters' contents would be different, since they had been rewritten. The returns to Haiti after travelling to the United States and the Dominican Republic

Respectfully, I am also of the opinion that the RPD erred in its conclusion that the appellant demonstrated behaviour inconsistent with that of a person fearing for her life by returning to Haiti after staying in the United States and the Dominican Republic. The appellant explained that she returned to Haiti after taking refuge in the United States from XXXX 2011 to XXXX 2011, because she believed that she could live in hiding. I am of the view that this explanation is acceptable, especially in the context of domestic abuse.

The RPD's other findings on the appellant's credibility also focused on elements that are not at the core of the appellant's refugee protection claim. In my view, the elements raised by the RPD in its decision are not sufficient to rebut the presumption of truthfulness of the appellant's testimony. Furthermore, the RPD ignored the credible aspects of the appellant's testimony as well as the documentary evidence corroborating her testimony.

After hearing the principal appellant testify about the abuse she experienced from 2009 to 2011 in Haiti at the hands of her former spouse, I am of the opinion that she is credible with regard to her fear of persecution in Haiti. Her testimony was spontaneous and detailed regarding the threats, attacks and harassment that she and her family received from her former spouse.3 I did not note any omissions or contradictions in this part of the testimony, which is the core of her refugee protection claim. Moreover, throughout the hearing, she answered the questions directly and did not try to embellish her story.
The RPD incorrectly found the appellant's testimony to be not credible. The Refugee Protection Division did not conduct the hearing in accordance with the principles of the Chairperson's Guideline 4

The RPD did not consider the principles of the Chairperson's Guideline 4 when assessing the appellant's refugee protection claim. During the hearing, the RPD did not apply Guideline 4 and make the necessary accommodations to hear the testimony of a person whose refugee protection claim is based on domestic violence. Even when the appellant had visible difficulty testifying about the abuse she experienced, no break was offered during the hearing, even when she burst into sobs.4 Yet, the appellant's record clearly states that she is a survivor of domestic violence and indicates the measures that should have been taken from the start of the hearing to respect the principles of the Chairperson's Guideline 4.

In its reasons and analysis, the RPD ignores the fact that survivors of domestic violence may suffer from post-traumatic stress. Even if it had doubts about the appellant's credibility, the RPD should have considered the effect that trauma related to domestic violence can have on a refugee protection claimant's testimony, which it did not do.

The RPD did not conduct the hearing or analyze the appellant's refugee protection claim in accordance with the principles of the Chairperson's Guideline 4. The Refugee Protection Division erred by not considering the documentary evidence The RPD erred by not giving probative value to the medical report.

I am of the view that the RPD erred by not giving probative value to the medical report submitted into evidence by the appellant. In paragraph 26 of its decision, the RPD states that the medical report is insufficient to offset the appellant's [translation] "...numerous credibility issues." However, I am of the opinion that the "credibility issues" raised by the RPD do not rebut the presumption of truth. Furthermore, the probative value of a medical report should not depend entirely on the appellant's credibility. Insofar as it is a genuine document, an analysis of its contents was necessary.

The author of this medical report is the doctor who saw and treated the eye injury inflicted by the appellant's former spouse. The report states that the appellant [translation] "suffered trauma to the left eye." 5 Although it cannot be ruled out that this injury may have been caused by an incident other than that alleged by the appellant, the diagnosis made in the medical report is consistent with her testimony. It is true that the report mentions an injury to the left eye, while the appellant refers to her right eye, but this is a minor element relating to an event that occurred in 2010. It would also be reasonable to believe that the doctor might have made a mistake when writing the report. I have no reason to conclude that this medical report is not genuine. In my opinion, it corroborates the appellant's testimony.

The other documentary evidence submitted by the appellant is also relevant in the analysis of her refugee protection claim, particularly, a letter from a counselor at an organization (HELP R.O.A.D.S) that assists survivors of domestic violence in the United States. This letter indicates that the appellant used their services and that she allegedly experienced a second abusive interaction with her husband in the United States. This information is relevant and should have been taken into account by the RPD in the analysis of the appellant's refugee protection claim, and accommodations should have been made to hear her refugee protection claim. Prospective risk in Haiti

The appellant credibly established that she experienced domestic abuse over many years, which has had a lasting effect and makes her more vulnerable. If the appellant were to return to Haiti, she fears physical abuse at the hands of her former spouse, who, do not forget, is also a police officer. I have no reason to doubt that she fears returning to Haiti because there is no protection for women who experience domestic violence.
On this subject, the documentary evidence states that domestic and spousal violence are widespread in Haiti, taking many forms, including insults, harassment and sexual violence.6

In my opinion, if the appellant had to return to live in Haiti, she would face more than a mere possibility of persecution because of her former spouse and her membership in the group of Haitian women. The fact that she is a survivor of domestic violence makes her particularly vulnerable to further violence. Lack of state protection

Sources state that "Haitian police have received some training in recent years and improvements are reported with regard to willingness of police to receive complaints." However, it also states that "in spite of these efforts, the credibility of the police remains limited" and that "women victims of violence who attempt to access the legal system face a number of obstacles."7

On this topic, Tab 5.3 of the National Documentation Package for Haiti states: ... Sources state that the justice system in Haiti fosters impunity...including with respect to violence against women. ... Haiti does not have specific legislation criminalizing rape, domestic violence, sexual harassment, or other forms of violence suffered by women. ... The Co-Legal Director at CGRS also stated that Penal Code provisions for battery and assault should also be applicable in cases of violence against women, but stated that "laws to punish perpetrators of violence against women, [...] are rarely enforced." The collective of university institutions and NGOs report that the Haitian justice system lacks support, including for responding to cases of violence against women.... The legal procedure is described as "complex, intimidating and sometimes hostile [towards female victims of violence]." 8

In the appellant's case, we have even more reason to doubt that the state could protect the appellant because her former spouse is a police officer. For these reasons, I conclude that the state would be unable to provide the appellant adequate protection if she returned to Haiti.

The appeal is allowed. I substitute own determination that the appellant is a Convention refugee.
